title: Chapter 2 — The Carpet-Bag
paragraphs: I stuffed a shirt or two into my old carpet-bag, tucked it under my arm, and headed for Cape Horn and the Pacific. Leaving the good city of old Manhatto, I duly arrived in New Bedford. It was a Saturday night in December. I was very disappointed to learn that the little packet boat to Nantucket had already sailed, and that there would be no way of getting there until the following Monday.

Since most young candidates for the pains and penalties of whaling stop at this same New Bedford, to embark on their voyage from there, I may as well say that I, for one, had no intention of doing so. My mind was made up to sail in nothing but a Nantucket craft, because there was a fine, boisterous something about everything connected with that famous old island that pleased me amazingly. Besides, though New Bedford has lately been gradually monopolizing the whaling business, and though poor old Nantucket is now far behind her in this matter, Nantucket was her great original — the Tyre of this Carthage — the place where the first dead American whale was stranded. Where else but from Nantucket did those aboriginal whalemen, the Red-Men, first sally out in canoes to give chase to the Leviathan? And where but from Nantucket, too, did that first adventurous little sloop set out, partly loaded with imported cobblestones — so the story goes — to throw at the whales, in order to find out when they were near enough to risk a harpoon from the bowsprit?

Now, with a night, a day, and still another night ahead of me in New Bedford before I could embark for my intended port, the question of where I was to eat and sleep in the meantime became a matter of concern. It was a very dubious-looking — no, a very dark and dismal — night, bitingly cold and cheerless. I knew no one in the place. With anxious grappling hooks I had sounded my pocket, and brought up only a few pieces of silver. So, wherever you go, Ishmael, I said to myself, as I stood in the middle of a dreary street shouldering my bag and comparing the gloom to the north with the darkness to the south — wherever in your wisdom you may decide to lodge for the night, my dear Ishmael, be sure to ask the price, and don't be too particular.

With halting steps I paced the streets, and passed the sign of "The Crossed Harpoons" — but it looked too expensive and jolly there. Farther on, from the bright red windows of the "Sword-Fish Inn" came such fervent rays that they seemed to have melted the packed snow and ice from in front of the house, for everywhere else the congealed frost lay ten inches thick in a hard, asphalt-like pavement — rather tiring for me when I struck my foot against the flinty ridges, because after hard, remorseless service the soles of my boots were in a most miserable state. Too expensive and jolly, I thought again, pausing a moment to watch the broad glare in the street and hear the tinkling of glasses inside. But go on, Ishmael, I said at last; don't you hear? Get away from the door; your patched boots are blocking the way. So on I went. I now followed by instinct the streets that led me toward the water, for there, no doubt, were the cheapest, if not the cheeriest, inns.

What dreary streets! Blocks of blackness, not houses, on either side, and here and there a candle, like a candle moving about in a tomb. At this hour of the night, on the last day of the week, that part of town proved all but deserted. But soon I came to a smoky light coming from a low, wide building, whose door stood invitingly open. It had a careless look, as if it were meant for the use of the public; so, going in, the first thing I did was stumble over an ash-box in the porch. Ha! I thought, ha, as the flying particles almost choked me — are these ashes from that destroyed city, Gomorrah? But "The Crossed Harpoons," and "The Sword-Fish"? — then this must be the sign of "The Trap." However, I picked myself up, and, hearing a loud voice inside, pushed on and opened a second, inner door.

It seemed like the great Black Parliament sitting in Tophet, the biblical hell. A hundred black faces turned around in their rows to peer; and beyond, a black Angel of Doom was beating a book in a pulpit. It was a negro church; and the preacher's text was about the blackness of darkness, and the weeping and wailing and teeth-gnashing there. Ha, Ishmael, I muttered, backing out — wretched entertainment at the sign of "The Trap"!

Moving on, I at last came to a dim sort of light not far from the docks and heard a forlorn creaking in the air. Looking up, I saw a swinging sign over the door with a white painting on it, faintly representing a tall, straight jet of misty spray, and these words underneath: "The Spouter Inn — Peter Coffin."

Coffin? Spouter? Rather ominous in that particular connection, I thought. But it's a common name in Nantucket, they say, and I suppose this Peter here is an emigrant from there. Since the light looked so dim, and the place looked quiet enough for the time being, and the dilapidated little wooden house itself looked as if it might have been carted here from the ruins of some burned district, and since the swinging sign had a poverty-stricken sort of creak to it, I thought this was the very spot for cheap lodgings and the best of pea coffee.

It was an odd sort of place — a gable-ended old house, one side palsied, as it were, and leaning over sadly. It stood on a sharp, bleak corner, where that tempestuous wind Euroclydon kept up a worse howling than it ever did around poor Paul's storm-tossed ship. Euroclydon, nevertheless, is a mighty pleasant breeze to anyone indoors, with his feet on the hearth, quietly toasting them before bed. "In judging of that tempestuous wind called Euroclydon," says an old writer — of whose works I possess the only surviving copy — "it makes a marvelous difference whether you look out at it from a glass window where the frost is all on the outside, or whether you observe it from that sashless window, where the frost is on both sides, and of which that fellow Death is the only glazier." True enough, I thought, as this passage came to mind — old black-letter book, you reason well. Yes, these eyes are windows, and this body of mine is the house. What a pity they didn't stop up the chinks and crannies, though, and stuff in a little lint here and there. But it's too late to make any improvements now. The universe is finished; the copestone is on, and the chips were carted off a million years ago. Poor Lazarus there, chattering his teeth against the curbstone for his pillow, and shaking off his tatters with his shivering — he might plug up both ears with rags and put a corncob in his mouth, and still that would not keep out the tempestuous Euroclydon. Euroclydon! says old Dives, in his red silk robe (he had a redder one afterward) — pooh, pooh! What a fine frosty night; how Orion glitters; what northern lights! Let them talk of their Eastern summer climates of everlasting conservatories; give me the privilege of making my own summer with my own coals.

But what does Lazarus think? Can he warm his blue hands by holding them up to the grand northern lights? Wouldn't Lazarus rather be in Sumatra than here? Wouldn't he far rather lay himself down lengthwise along the line of the equator — yes, you gods! — even go down to the fiery pit itself, to keep out this frost?

Now, that Lazarus should be lying stranded there on the curb outside Dives's door is more astonishing than if an iceberg were moored to one of the Moluccas. And yet Dives himself also lives like a czar in an ice palace built of frozen sighs, and since he is president of a temperance society, the only thing he drinks is the lukewarm tears of orphans.
But no more of this blubbering now — we're going whaling, and there's plenty of that still to come. Let's scrape the ice from our frosted feet and see what sort of place this "Spouter" may be.
